title: Chapter 197 – The Cost of Mending
html:
[The Dock and the Clan Gate – Lin Jian]

The cup shakes before Jian knows his hand has moved.

He sets it down on the kitchen table with a click, and the tea inside it slops over the rim and spreads across the boards. For a moment he looks at the puddle. Then he looks at the hand, the left one, with its long scarred fingers and the silver line of old Gate-burn across the knuckles, and he watches it tremble in the morning light like a leaf on a still pond.

He has not had a tremor before. He has had a great deal else: the cough that wakes him every night, the weight in the chest, the nausea after he climbs stairs. Those he can account for. They come from a Core that was grown in a hurry from the heart of a dead beast, and from the long cold run home, and from a body that is, by any honest reckoning, a hundred and nineteen years old. But the tremor is new. It arrived three days ago, between one breath and the next, while he was reading a ledger. He told nobody.

"You are spilling," says Bell.

"I know."

"I would not make a fuss, but the tea is Qinghe's, and she will count the leaves."

Bell sits across from him, small and brisk in a mended gown, with her black wax pills in a tray at her elbow. She is not looking at his hand. She is looking at his face with the particular flat attention she gives to a patient who has told her it is nothing. She has been the Hall's healer for six weeks and the clan's before that, and in all that time she has never once been told the truth the first time.

"Roll up your sleeve," she says.

"It is only the cold."

"Roll it up, Head Lin."

He does. She takes his wrist in two dry fingers and holds it for the space of twenty breaths. Her lips move as she counts. Her eyes close. When they open again, the flatness has gone out of them.

"Your pulse is a mess," she says.

"That is a medical term?"

"It is my term." She lets go. "Three beats and a skip. Two beats and a stumble. It has been doing that since the Wall, I think, and the pills have been hiding it. They are not hiding it any longer."

"How long?"

"Weeks. Perhaps less." She sets her jaw. "You know what I am going to say."

"That I should rest."

"That you should stop. Not rest. Stop. Put down the staff, put down the Roll, put down the Nine, and lie in a bed for a year with someone feeding you broth. You have a hole in your chest the size of my fist, Jian. I can feel it through the skin."

He is silent. In the corner of his sight, small and pale, the panel he has been avoiding all morning gives a patient flicker.

"I cannot stop," he says at last.

"No. I did not think so." She picks up the tray. "Then you had better think of something cleverer than broth."

* * *

The thing he thinks of is the Print.

He does not like it. He has never liked the Interface's quieter powers, the ones that do not announce themselves with a bright cost. Scan, he understands. Scan is a lantern. It shows what is there. Print is a hand. It makes what is not, and a hand can slip.

But the Hall is quiet at noon. The Seven are at their lessons in the Roll Room with Zhao, who has discovered, to his own astonishment, that he enjoys teaching. The sleepers who woke yesterday are being fed in the long gallery by a dozen volunteers. And Jian, with his staff in his right hand and his left hidden in his sleeve, goes down the Dock stair alone to a small stone chamber that no one else in the valley has yet found a reason to visit.

It is a round room, empty, with a floor of bare black stone and a ceiling of nothing. Mo Yan found it by accident. She says it has been waiting. There is a drain in the center for water, and a ring of low stone benches round the wall, and a faint smell of cold iron, like the inside of a forge long unlit. He sits on the nearest bench. He lays the staff across his knees.

Show me, he thinks.

```
ARK-7 // PRINT
STATUS: UNLOCKED (ARK-6 KEY ACCEPTED)
MODE: SELF-REPAIR (LIVING TISSUE, HOST)
TARGET: MOONHORN CORE, LATTICE DAMAGE (79% INTEGRITY)
PROPOSED: PRINT 11% OF LATTICE FROM HOST MARROW AND CORE RESIDUE
REQUIRES ......... 3 DAYS BEDREST (HOST)
COST (LIFESPAN) .. 2 YEARS
COST (MATTER) .... 410 GRAMS HOST MARROW (REGENERATES)
COST (TEMPLATE) .. SEE NOTE
NOTE: PRINT USES A PATTERN TEMPLATE. NO TEMPLATE OF HOST CORE EXISTS.
NEAREST AVAILABLE TEMPLATE: THE NINE-RING (SHARED).
```

He reads it twice. He reads the last note three times.

The Nine-Ring, he thinks. The thing the children made last week. The thing that holds the Hall.

```
ARK-7 // EXPLANATION
THE NINE-RING IS A SHARED PATTERN BANK.
PRINT MAY DRAW ON IT AS A TEMPLATE, WITH THE CONSENT OF ITS HOLDERS.
CONSENT STATUS: HOLDER 8 (HOST) ... GRANTED.
HOLDERS 1-7, 9 ..... NOT ASKED.
DRAWING WITHOUT CONSENT: PERMITTED.
DRAWING WITHOUT CONSENT: CHARGED TO HOLDERS IN PROPORTION TO SPARE CAPACITY.
SPARE CAPACITY (HOLDER 9): 6%.
```

His mouth goes dry.

In proportion to spare capacity. He does the sum without wanting to. Mei is the one with the least to spare. If the Print draws on the ring without asking, the cost falls on the one who can least afford it.

And if I ask them?

```
ARK-7 // REPLY
CONSENT FROM A HOLDER SHIFTS COST TO THAT HOLDER'S CHOICE OF ALLOCATION.
HOLDERS MAY SPLIT THE COST EVENLY OR DECLINE.
THE HOST HAS NOT ASKED.
```

"Of course I have not asked," Jian says aloud, softly, to the empty room. His voice echoes off the stone. "I am not an idiot. I know what they would say."

They would say yes, he thinks. All of them. At once. And Mei would insist on taking the lion's share.

He sits there a long time with his hands on his knees. Above him the not-ceiling holds a few pale stars. Somewhere on the far side of the Hall a woman is laughing. Nobody has ever laughed in this room.

Then he stands, and goes to find the Nine.

* * *

On the way up he meets Kuang in the lowest gallery.

The boy is thirteen, heir to a clan that numbers nine hundred and forty-three adopted orphans and a little over a thousand living blood, and he carries his responsibilities the way a small man carries a large sack: with elaborate care and no visible notion of how to put it down. He is walking with a slate under one arm and a stub of chalk behind his ear, and when he sees Jian his face goes through three expressions in a second, the last of which is stern.

"Uncle," he says. "You are out of bed."

"So I am told."

"Bell said three days."

"Everyone says that."

"Because it is true." Kuang straightens. "I came to report. The Roll stands at two thousand and eleven names, the Seven included. Zhao says the grain will last until the first thaw if the Wall's wagons do not fail. The Elders have asked if the clan may hold a funeral for the Night of Counting. They want to name the dead aloud."

"Is it time?"

"They think so." The boy hesitates. "I did not know whether to ask you. I am Heir. I think I am supposed to decide. But I do not think I know how."

Jian studies him. The chalk behind the ear. The ink on the left cuff. The anxious sharp jaw that belongs, he realizes, to Zhao Yao at the same age, before the Sect and the Night and the long climb that made her a stranger.

"What do you want to do?" he says.

"I want to do it." Kuang's voice is steady. "But I want it to be right. They were people. They should not be a number on a slate."

"Then that is your answer."

"It is?"

"It is the only answer I have ever found worth following." Jian lays a hand on the thin shoulder. "Hold the funeral. Name them. Let each family say the name of its own. And let the Heir stand at the back, not the front, and listen."

Kuang blinks. A slow, startled smile crosses his face, the first Jian has seen from him in a month.

"At the back," he says.

"A clan leader who stands at the back hears who is missing."

The boy nods. He writes something on his slate, very carefully, in block letters, and Jian reads over his shoulder: STAND AT THE BACK. Underneath, smaller: LISTEN.

They give him the answer he expected, and he hates it.

He gathers them in the Council Chamber that evening, all nine chairs, and the tenth stool with the firewood back. He tells them plainly: the core, the print, the cost. He does not dress it. He watches their faces while he speaks, and sees the moment it lands. Duan Ke's jaw tightens. Zhen Li puts a fist to her mouth. Cheng Hui folds his hands very carefully on the stone.

"Say it again," says Hai Ren. "The part about the template."

"The Interface needs a pattern to copy. It does not have one of my core. It has one of the Nine-Ring. If I print from the ring, the pattern will be a blend of all of ours."

"Of us."

"Of you. A little of each." He rubs his eyes. "It would not change you. But it would change me. The repair would carry traces. How much, I cannot say."

"What traces?"

"I do not know."

"And the cost to us?"

"A little. Spread. Or a great deal to Mei, if I take it unasked." He turns toward her. "I will not take it unasked."

Mei is sitting on the ninth chair with her feet tucked under her. She is a little brighter than she was yesterday, a faint steady silver, and the leaf from the Mother Tree lies in her lap like a coin. She has not spoken since he began.

"Is it true you'll die if you don't?" she says.

"I will die sooner."

"How soon?"

"Weeks, Bell thinks. Months, if I am careful."

"And if you are careful, and you do it, how long?"

"Years." He swallows. "Perhaps a good many."

"Then there's nothing to decide," says Mei, simply.

"There is a great deal to decide. It is your pattern. It is all of yours." He looks round the circle. "I cannot ask you to give up even a day. Not after last week. Not after..."

"Jian."

It is Mo Yan. She has risen. She stands at the end of the ring with her braid in her hand, small and solemn, and for a moment he does not understand what she is doing. She lifts her palm. She turns it toward him, flat.

"She says yes," murmurs Yue, from the wall. She has been leaning there with her arms folded since the first word. "She says she would give a hundred days."

"A day is plenty," says Cheng Hui, hoarsely. He has not looked up. "A day from each of us. Split evenly. No lion's share."

"I won't have it," says Mei.

"You'll have it," says Hai Ren. "You said it yourself. We share."

Mei opens her mouth, and shuts it. Her gray eyes go very wide and bright. She pulls her feet up onto the chair and wraps her arms round her knees.

"Fine," she says, very small. "But I get to be cross about it."

"You may be as cross as you like."

"I'm very cross."

"I can tell," says Jian, and does not trust himself to say more.

* * *

Pebble comes to him before the print, as he knew she would.

She has been quiet for weeks. A pangolin the size of a house cat, in a cloak of hard bronze scales that clink when she moves, she has spent the long recovery curled in the hollow of his cloak, warm against his ribs, saying nothing. Beasts of her bloodline do not speak until Nascent Soul. She has made her peace with that. She has also, he knows, made her own judgments, which she expresses with her tail.

Tonight she uncurls on the surgery table and fixes him with her black bead eyes.

What? he asks.

She does not answer. She climbs onto his chest, deliberately, and settles with her nose against his chin. He feels the whole small hot weight of her. He feels a slow, firm, unmistakable thought go through the bond between them, as clear as a spoken word:

Do not go where I cannot follow.

"I am not going anywhere," he says.

The scales rattle. A snort.

"I am not. It is a repair. Eleven hours."

Another snort. Her claws flex, once, against his collar. The thought comes again, slower, with a heaviness he has not felt from her before, and he understands that it is not about the print at all.

The big door. The one with the number. You will go. And I will be small, and I will not be able to speak, and I will not be able to hold it shut when it opens.

"Pebble—"

Take me.

He is silent. It is not a request. It is a statement of fact, offered in the dry, level voice of an animal that has walked through the dark under the earth for six hundred years and has never once been wrong about where a seam was going to open.

"I will," he says. "When it is time. I swear it."

She does not answer. She only presses her scaly head under his chin and goes still, and in a moment she is purring, faintly, like a kettle.

The print takes eleven hours, and he remembers almost none of them.

He is on his back on a cot in Bell's surgery, with a strip of black cloth over his eyes and his hands strapped loosely at his sides, and the room smells of camphor and warm wax. Bell sits at his head. She holds a bowl of cold water and a cloth, and every few minutes she wets his lips. Yue sits at his feet, saying nothing, with her good hand curled round his ankle. He can feel its warmth through the blanket.

The Interface speaks in whispers.

```
PRINT: INITIALIZING
TEMPLATE: NINE-RING (SPLIT EVEN, 1 DAY EACH)
SOURCE: HOST MARROW, 410 G
RATE: 0.4% LATTICE / HOUR
...
LATTICE 79% -> 81%
...
LATTICE 81% -> 86%
...
WARNING: TRACE ADMIXTURE DETECTED
WARNING: TRACE SOURCE: HOLDER 1-7 (BLOOD-FAULT MARKER)
WARNING: MARKER IS HEREDITARY (LIN LINE)
WARNING: HOST CARRIES LIN LINE.
```

Of course I do, he thinks, from a long way off. I am a Lin. I was born in this valley. The Warden chose eight of us.

```
PRINT: COMPLETE
LATTICE: 91%
LIFESPAN: 105Y 213D -> 103Y 213D
HOLDER COST (EACH, 1-9): 1 DAY. LOGGED.
SIDE EFFECT (PERMANENT): INTENTION TREMOR, LEFT HAND (LIN MARKER, MILD)
SIDE EFFECT (PERMANENT): MARKER PRESENT IN PRINT TEMPLATE. FUTURE PRINTS WILL CARRY IT.
```

He drifts. At some point Bell removes the cloth. At some point Yue's hand tightens on his ankle. At some point the room grows dark, then bright, then dark again, and he hears someone singing, a thin, flat, tuneless thing like a cat yawning. He realizes, dimly, that it is himself.

On the third day he opens his eyes and the cough is gone.

* * *

The wagons leave at the new moon, on a gray morning with a high wind.

The clan gate is crowded. Forty wagons, empty now, stand in a double line down the road, their mules stamping and blowing. Han's drivers are checking harnesses. A knot of Lins has gathered round the foremost, and in the middle of it, in their traveling cloaks, with two small bundles at their feet, stand Wenyuan and Qinghe.

Jian does not run. He cannot yet. He walks, with the staff, along the line of mules, and the clan opens before him like water.

"You are up," says Wenyuan, gruffly.

"I am up."

"Bell said three days."

"It was three days."

"It looks like thirty." His father studies him, and the stern lines in his face ease a little. "But you are standing, which is more than I expected."

"I wanted to see you off."

"We are not leaving forever."

"No." Jian looks at the wagons, the wind, the long gray road. "But you are leaving."

Qinghe puts down her bundle. She is wearing the blue smock she has worn for forty years, patched at the elbows, and over it a heavy brown cloak that smells of wood smoke and bread. She steps close, and before he can say anything she takes his left hand in both of hers.

He tries to pull it away. He is too slow.

She holds it. She holds it in the palm of her own broad warm hand, and her thumb moves slowly across the back of it, over the scar, over the knuckles, and then stops. He feels the tremor. He sees her feel it. For a long moment she does not say anything at all.

"That is new," she says.

"It is nothing."

"It is not nothing. It is a Lin tremor. My mother's brother had it, and his daughter." Her voice is quiet. "It runs in the line. It does not come to a person without a cause."

"Mother—"

"I am not asking you what you did." She looks up. Her eyes are dark and clear and very tired. "I am asking whether you chose it."

He thinks of the room, the cot, the cloth over his eyes. He thinks of Mo Yan's raised palm.

"I chose it," he says.

"Knowing?"

"Knowing most of it."

She nods slowly. She does not let go of his hand. "Then you chose well enough," she says. "Mind that you eat."

"I will."

"Do not tell me you will. Tell me who is going to make you."

"Yue."

"Good." A grim little smile. "She has her father's temper. Do not argue with her."

He laughs. It rattles in his chest, but it does not cough. Wenyuan, standing beside them with his arms folded, makes a gruff sound in his throat that might be impatience and might be something else.

"The Wall will want us before dark," he says. "If we are going."

"Go."

"We will write."

"I know."

"Write back."

"I will write back." Jian steps forward, awkwardly, and puts his arms round his father. The old man stiffens. Then he returns the embrace, a hard crushing grip that smells of leather and cold air, and says, close to his ear, so that no one else can hear:

"You should not have to do this alone."

"I am not alone."

"That is not what I said."

He lets go. He steps back. The wagons are filling now, drivers swinging up onto the boxes, Han's guard in their gray cloaks lined up beside the road. Qinghe is already climbing onto the first seat, helped up by a broad red-faced woman with a scar under one eye. She settles her skirts. She looks down at him once, over the side, and lifts her hand.

The mules lean into the harness. The wheels groan. The wagons begin to roll, one after another, down the road toward the pass, and the wind catches the canvas and billows it like a long gray sail.

He watches until the last wagon has gone. Then he turns, and finds Yue at his elbow.

"You are shaking," she says.

"It is the wind."

"It is not the wind." She takes his arm. "Come. Bell has soup."

* * *

Cheng Hui finds him on the Dock stair that night, and sits down two steps below.

He says nothing for a while. He has a way of doing that, a courtesy of silence that Jian has come to value more than any speech. The lamps burn low. Below them the Hall breathes, ring on ring of sleepers, and one new light, near the bottom, where yesterday's sleeper lies sleeping off her first meal.

"I wanted to say," says Cheng Hui at last, "that I felt it."

"Felt what?"

"The day. When you printed." He rubs his own hands together, slowly, and Jian sees them tremble in the lamplight. "It was like a cold hand on the back of my neck. And then nothing. It was only a day. I did not mind it."

"You should have minded."

"I did not." The boy looks up. His face is thin and grave and older than nineteen. "I wanted to tell you something I did not say in the Council. When the Interface told you the print would carry the marker, you went white. I saw it. You thought we would be angry."

"Were you not?"

"No." A very small smile. "We have had it all our lives. We hid it in our sleeves. You will hide it too, and then one day you will stop, and nobody will notice, because we all have it. It is not a flaw. It is a family trait."

Jian looks at his own left hand. It lies quiet on his knee. It has not trembled since morning.

"A family trait," he says.

"Welcome to it," says Cheng Hui.

Jian laughs. He cannot help it. It comes up from somewhere deep and rusty, and it hurts, and he goes on laughing until his eyes sting. Cheng Hui joins him, shyly, and then they are both laughing like two fools on a stair at midnight, and below them a small lamp flickers in the dark.

* * *

It is Mei who tells him the rest, much later, when the Hall is still.

She comes to the surgery where he lies awake. She is a faint pale glimmer at the foot of his cot. She does not say hello. She sits on the end of the blanket, as lightly as a bird, and looks at him with her old gray eyes.

"I counted," she says.

"Counted what?"

"The days. When you printed. I felt each one go." Her voice is steady. "A day each, evenly, like you said. I wasn't cross after all. I thought it would be worse."

"Good."

"But there was one more."

He goes still.

"One more day," says Mei. "From me. At the very end, after the others had finished. It wasn't taken. It was just... gone." She tilts her head. "Like a coin falling out of a purse. I think the ring is leaking."

"The Nine-Ring?"

"A little." She says it so carefully that he knows she has been rehearsing. "Every time you print, it'll leak. Not much. But I'm the weakest link. I'm the one that gives."

He sits up. The room swims. He reaches for the panel with a thought, and it opens at once, as if it had been waiting for him to ask.

```
ARK-7 // AUDIT
NINE-RING STABILITY: 96.8% (-0.4% THIS PRINT)
HOLDER 9 (MEI) SPARE CAPACITY: 5% (-1%)
CAUSE: PRINT DRAWS ON THE RING MORE THAN IT REPORTS.
NOTE: THIS UNIT WAS BUILT TO DRAW ON THE RING.
NOTE: THIS UNIT WAS BUILT FOR NINE HOSTS.
NOTE: THIS UNIT HAS ONLY ONE.
```

He reads it. He reads it again. The cold spreads through his chest like water through sand.

Built for nine hosts.

"Jian?" says Mei.

He says nothing. He is looking at the last line of the panel, which has begun to scroll slowly upward, line by line, in a hand he has never seen before.

```
ARK-7 // MEMORY INDEX
SHARD 4: READABLE
ACCESS: GRANTED (NINE-RING CONSENT, 8 OF 9)
HOLDER 9 CONSENT: PENDING.
```

Across the room, the lamp gutters. Mei's glow trembles on the blanket.

"Do you want to know?" she says, so softly he can barely hear. "I can say yes. It would only cost me a day."
